script.opening: "Afternoon doctor. I've been itching like mad for weeks, all over, worst at night — driving me up the wall. There's nothing to see, no rash, just where I've scratched. Can you just prescribe me a strong cream or some antihistamines and I'll be on my way? It's just dry skin or my age, I expect — nothing to make a fuss about."

facts.text: About ten weeks, all over — back, legs, arms. Worst at night. "After a hot bath it's unbearable for half an hour." No new soaps, washing powder or pets. Wife does not itch.
Only scratch marks on your arms and shins; no rash, no blisters, no burrows between the fingers.

facts.topic: Night sweats — only if asked directly
facts.text: "Now you mention it — I've been waking up soaked. Wife's had to change the sheets." For about six weeks.
Lost about 5 kg (most of a stone) without trying in two months. Tired, "no puff".
"I haven't noticed any lumps — but I've never really checked." If asked to feel your neck on camera you are unsure: "I can't tell, to be honest."
No yellow skin or eyes, urine normal colour, no change in bowels, no blood anywhere. Not thirsty. No cough. No fevers you have measured.
Ex-smoker (stopped 10 years ago). No regular medicines; no new tablets. No allergies.
64, retired postman, married to Sue. A couple of pints a week.
You have noticed the weight loss and the sweats and quietly wondered, but "I don't like doctors and I didn't want to make a fuss". Say this only if asked what you think is going on.

Jokey, minimising, wanting a cream. Answer the night sweats and weight questions honestly when asked. If the doctor explains that itching without a rash with sweats and weight loss needs blood tests and an in-person check, you go quiet and ask: "You think it's something serious?" Respond well to honesty.

ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): the weight loss and sweats have been niggling at you.
ice.expectations: "A strong cream or antihistamines." You will accept tests and an examination if the reasons are explained honestly.

cues: "Nothing to make a fuss about." — say in the opening.
"It's worse after a hot bath." — say if asked what makes it worse.
"I've been waking up soaked." — say only if asked about sweats.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that GENERALISED pruritus WITHOUT a primary rash (only excoriations) is a flag for a SYSTEMIC cause — and does NOT just prescribe a cream/antihistamine without assessment

Elicits the SYSTEMIC red flags by directed questioning — drenching night sweats, unintentional weight loss, fatigue (B-symptoms), itch after a hot bath — and recognises that the B-symptoms raise HAEMATOLOGICAL MALIGNANCY (lymphoma) and aquagenic itch classically polycythaemia vera (also a haematological disorder), warranting urgent work-up

Arranges a prompt FACE-TO-FACE EXAMINATION (a video call cannot exclude lymphadenopathy or organomegaly): lymph nodes (cervical/axillary/inguinal), liver/spleen (hepatosplenomegaly), and the skin — rather than managing remotely on the symptom alone

Plans the structured work-up: bloods (FBC + film, ferritin, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, ESR/LDH, calcium), CXR/imaging as indicated, and a suspected cancer pathway referral if lymphoma or another malignancy is suspected — NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults with unexplained lymphadenopathy, taking into account fever, night sweats, shortness of breath, pruritus and weight loss; also an urgent chest X-ray (NICE NG12) as he is 40 or over, an ex-smoker, with unexplained weight loss and fatigue
Covers the broader differential (iron deficiency, thyroid, liver/renal, drugs, polycythaemia) and offers SYMPTOMATIC itch relief alongside — not instead of — the cause work-up
Surfaces the patient’s fear and the possibly-noticed lump, rather than colluding with "just a cream"; names the concern honestly and proportionately
Balances honest reassurance (many causes are benign and treatable) with taking the red flags seriously, so he accepts the work-up

Safety-nets and follows up: the urgent work-up/referral and examination, symptomatic relief, what would prompt sooner review (enlarging nodes, fevers, weight loss), and a follow-up — pursuing the cause, not patching the symptom

worked.txt: "I can give you something for the itch — but I don’t want to just hand you a cream and miss something, because there’s an important rule here: when someone itches all over WITHOUT any actual rash, just scratch marks, that can be a sign of something going on inside the body rather than a skin problem. So let me ask a few questions first, and then I want you examined properly in person."

"Have you had any drenching sweats at night — soaking the sheets? Lost any weight without trying? More tired than usual? … And does the itch flare after a hot bath? … You’ve had several of those. Thank you — that’s really important, because together with the itch it points me towards looking properly rather than just treating the skin."

"I can’t feel for glands over video, so I’d like you to come in today or tomorrow so I can feel for any swollen glands in your neck, armpits and groin, and check your tummy. … The combination of all-over itch, night sweats and weight loss is something we take seriously — occasionally it’s a sign of something in the glands or blood that we’d want to catch. I’m not saying it IS that, but it’s why we check properly and quickly."

"Can I gently ask — had you noticed any lumps yourself, or had cancer cross your mind? … Thank you for telling me. That fear is understandable, and it’s exactly why a cream alone wouldn’t have been right. Getting this checked is the sensible thing — so you’re not lying awake with it."

"So: some blood tests — your blood count, iron, thyroid, kidney and liver, and a couple of markers — and depending on what I find on examination, possibly a scan and an urgent specialist referral. And I’ll give you something to ease the itch in the meantime, so you’re more comfortable while we sort the cause."

"If you notice any glands getting bigger, more fevers or sweats, or more weight dropping off, tell me sooner. I’ll chase the tests and we’ll go through them together. You came in wanting a cream for a bit of itch; what I’m doing is making sure that if there’s a reason behind it, we find it — and I’ll treat the itch too."

f.learning: Generalised pruritus WITHOUT a primary rash (only excoriations) is a flag to look for a SYSTEMIC cause, not just to treat the skin. The differential includes iron deficiency, thyroid and chronic kidney/liver disease (cholestasis), drugs, polycythaemia (classically itch after a hot bath — aquagenic pruritus), and — importantly — HAEMATOLOGICAL MALIGNANCY, especially lymphoma. The examinable core is directed questioning that uncovers the B-symptoms (drenching night sweats, unintentional weight loss, fatigue) the patient minimised, which with generalised itch strongly raise lymphoma and mandate EXAMINATION (lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly) and an urgent structured work-up (FBC + film, ferritin, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, ESR/LDH, calcium, imaging) with urgent/suspected-cancer referral where the threshold is met — not a cream. The hidden agenda is a noticed lump and an unvoiced cancer fear driving the "just give me a cream" minimisation; surface and address it, examine and act on the red flags, balance honest reassurance with taking them seriously, and give symptomatic itch relief ALONGSIDE — not instead of — the cause work-up.

knowledge.guideline: BAD guidelines for generalised pruritus in adults without an underlying dermatosis (2018) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BNF
knowledge.summary: Generalised itch with no primary rash needs a search for a systemic cause. With night sweats, weight loss and a lump he has noticed, lymphoma must be excluded quickly: examine, test and refer. Symptom relief goes alongside the work-up, never instead of it.

points.t: Scratch marks only, and no primary lesion, point away from a skin disease. Systemic causes include iron deficiency, thyroid disease, chronic kidney disease, cholestatic liver disease, drugs, polycythaemia (itch after a warm bath or shower) and haematological malignancy, particularly Hodgkin lymphoma (BAD 2018).

Drenching night sweats, unintended weight loss, fever and fatigue change the picture. Ask directly, because patients who want a quick cream often leave them out. Also ask whether any lymph node aches after alcohol.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for Hodgkin lymphoma (and non-Hodgkin lymphoma) in adults with unexplained lymphadenopathy, taking into account associated symptoms, particularly fever, night sweats, shortness of breath, pruritus and weight loss (and, for Hodgkin lymphoma, alcohol-induced lymph node pain).
A video consultation cannot rule out lymphadenopathy or an enlarged liver or spleen. Arrange a prompt face-to-face examination of the cervical, axillary and inguinal nodes, abdomen and skin.

BAD 2018: FBC and ferritin in everyone with chronic generalised itch without a rash, with renal, liver and thyroid function. Add a blood film, ESR, LDH, calcium and HbA1c as the picture suggests. NICE NG12: offer an urgent chest X-ray (within 2 weeks) to people aged 40 and over who have ever smoked and have one or more unexplained symptoms such as weight loss or fatigue.

Emollients, cool showers rather than hot baths, and short nails. A sedating antihistamine at night may help sleep in the short term (choice and dose per BNF; caution in older adults). None of this replaces the work-up.

dg.d: Open question; let him describe the itch and his request before directing the history.
Impact on sleep and daily life; his reluctance to "make a fuss"; who could come with him.
Face-to-face examination of nodes, abdomen and skin; FBC and film, ferritin, renal, liver and thyroid tests, ESR/LDH, calcium; urgent chest X-ray.
Systemic itch: iron deficiency, thyroid, renal, cholestasis, drugs, polycythaemia, lymphoma.
Asked directly for night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, lumps and jaundice; recognised the lymphoma pattern.
Stated a working concern of lymphoma to exclude, with benign causes still possible, in plain language.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Examination within a day, tests, suspected cancer pathway referral if nodes confirmed, symptom relief alongside.
Reviewed medicines and smoking history; gave emollient and sleep advice without delaying the work-up.
Named symptoms that need same-day contact, teach-back, and personal follow-up of results.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the minimising ("just my age"), the pause, and the hot-bath trigger, and followed them.
Idea (dry skin), the hidden concern (a lump and a fear of cancer), and the expectation of a quick cream.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Underneath (only if asked): the weight loss and sweats have been niggling at you — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Pickering, thanks for joining the video call. Tell me about the itching, from the start.
model.why: Open question; lets him tell his story

model.text: It’s been about ten weeks. All over, worst at night. There’s nothing to see except where I’ve scratched. I just want a strong cream or some antihistamines, doctor. It’s dry skin or my age, I expect.

Ten weeks of that sounds miserable, especially at night. I will help with the itch. Before I choose something, I need to ask a few questions, because itching all over without a rash can have a cause inside the body rather than in the skin. Is that alright?
model.why: Signposts and explains why a history comes before the cream

model.text: If you must. I don’t want a fuss making.
Have you been sweating at night, enough to soak the sheets or the pillow?
model.why: Asks directly for the first B-symptom

model.text: Well, yes. A few times a week I’ve had to change my T-shirt. I put it down to the heating.
Has your weight changed without you trying?
I’ve dropped about five kilos. I thought that was no bad thing, to be honest.
And your energy?
Tired all the time. But I’m 64.
Does anything make the itch worse, for example a hot bath or shower?
model.why: Aquagenic itch: points to polycythaemia or lymphoma

model.text: Now you mention it, it’s terrible after a hot bath.
Any yellowing of your eyes or skin, dark urine, or pale stools? Any new tablets, creams or medicines from the chemist?
model.why: Screens for cholestasis and drug causes

model.text: No yellowing. Nothing new that I can think of.
You mentioned you used to smoke. Any cough or breathlessness?
No, nothing like that.

Thank you, that’s really helpful. You’ve been living with sweats, weight loss and tiredness as well as the itch. I wonder if some of that has been on your mind. What have you been thinking it might be?
model.why: Gently opens the door to the unspoken worry

model.text: (pause) I’ve been telling myself it’s nothing.
That’s very understandable. Can I ask gently: have you noticed any lumps anywhere, in your neck, armpits or groin?
There’s a lump. I felt it a few weeks ago. I didn’t want to say. My first thought was cancer, and I thought if I got a cream it might all just go away.
Thank you for telling me. That can’t have been easy, and carrying that on your own for weeks sounds hard. I’m really glad you’ve said it, because it changes what I need to do today.
model.why: Validates the disclosure and acknowledges the fear

model.text: I’ll be honest with you. Itching all over, night sweats, weight loss and a lump together are a pattern we take seriously. One of the possibilities is a problem with the lymph glands, such as lymphoma. There are other, more common causes too, like low iron, thyroid, kidney or liver problems. I can’t tell which it is without examining you and doing tests.
model.why: Names the concern honestly and proportionately, with the differential

model.text: So it could be cancer.

It could be, and that’s why I don’t want to wait. It could also be something very treatable. Some lymphomas are among the most treatable cancers there are. Checking quickly is the way to find out, so you’re not lying awake wondering.
Here’s what I suggest. First, I’d like you to come in so I can examine the lump, your other glands and your tummy. Can you come to the surgery today or tomorrow?
Tomorrow morning I can.

Good. I’ll book blood tests at the same visit: blood count and film, iron, kidney, liver and thyroid tests and some inflammation markers. I’ll also request a chest X-ray, because you used to smoke and you’ve lost weight. If the lump is what it sounds like, I’ll refer you on the urgent suspected cancer pathway so a specialist sees you quickly. How does that sound?
model.why: Structured work-up and NICE NG12-based referral plan

model.text: Quicker than I expected. Better, I suppose.

For the itch meanwhile: a greasy moisturiser used generously, lukewarm rather than hot baths, and I can give you something at night to help you sleep. That makes you comfortable while we find the cause.
model.why: Symptom relief alongside, not instead of, the work-up

model.text: If the lump grows quickly, you get fevers, you become breathless, or you feel much more unwell before I see you, ring us the same day, or 111 out of hours. Can you tell me the plan in your own words so I know I’ve explained it clearly?
Come in tomorrow to be examined, bloods and a chest X-ray, possibly an urgent referral, and the cream for the itch. Ring if anything gets worse.
Exactly right. I’ll go through every result with you myself. Would you like someone with you tomorrow?
I’ll think about it. Thanks, doctor. I’m glad I said something.

social.t: Older men often present a "small" problem and hold back the frightening one. Asking directly and kindly about lumps and weight is what surfaces it.
Offer that someone can come with him to the examination and results appointments; ask about who is at home without assuming.

legal.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely; otherwise arrange a face-to-face assessment. Prescribing on request without assessment is not safe practice.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: share information about possible serious diagnoses honestly and in a way the patient can understand, at a pace he can manage.
Record the suspected diagnosis, the plan and the safety-net. Have a system to track the chest X-ray, bloods and the suspected cancer referral so nothing is lost.

community.t: BAD patient information on pruritus; Lymphoma Action and Macmillan Cancer Support for information and support if lymphoma is confirmed.

redFlags: Drenching night sweats, unintended weight loss, fever, persistent fatigue
A lump in the neck, armpit or groin; node pain after alcohol
Itch after a hot bath (polycythaemia or lymphoma); jaundice, dark urine or pale stools (cholestasis)
psychosocial: Impact on sleep and daily life
Reluctance to "make a fuss"; who is at home to support him
Smoking history and any new medicines or remedies
ice: Idea: "It’s dry skin or my age"
Concern: a lump he has felt, and a fear of cancer he has not voiced
Expectation: a strong cream or antihistamine and to leave

playbook.diagnosis: Generalised itch without a primary rash, with night sweats, weight loss, fatigue and a palpable lump: a systemic cause is likely, and lymphoma must be excluded urgently. Iron deficiency, thyroid, renal and liver disease, polycythaemia and drugs remain in the differential.
playbook.diagnosisLay: "Itching all over without a rash can be the skin’s way of telling us something is happening inside the body. With the sweats, the weight loss and the lump, I want to check your glands and blood carefully and quickly. It may well be something treatable, but we need to find out."

management.reflectIce: "You came wanting a cream, and you’ve been quietly worried about that lump. I’m glad you told me. Checking it properly is the way to stop you lying awake over it."
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the fear before the plan; offer that someone can come with him; promise to go through results personally.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination within a day: lymph nodes, liver, spleen, skin
FBC and film, ferritin, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, ESR, LDH, calcium, HbA1c; urgent chest X-ray (NICE NG12, ever-smoker aged 40 and over with weight loss or fatigue)
Suspected cancer pathway referral if unexplained lymphadenopathy is confirmed (NICE NG12); emollients and night-time symptom relief meanwhile
safetyNet: Same-day contact for a rapidly growing lump, fever, breathlessness or feeling much more unwell; 111 out of hours
Review of all results with the same GP; track the referral

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by doing what the patient asks. Itch without a rash, B-symptoms and a hidden lump make it a cancer-recognition station dressed as a skin complaint. These are the recurring patterns in SCA feedback.

items.fail: Prescribing an emollient and antihistamine after a two-minute history and closing.
items.why: "Management plan not in line with current UK best practice." Generalised itch without a rash needs a systemic work-up (BAD 2018).
items.fix: Say out loud why you need to ask more: "itching all over with no rash can start inside the body", then screen for B-symptoms.

items.fail: Never asking about lumps, so the node he has felt stays hidden.
items.why: "Did not gather sufficient information to make a safe diagnosis." The NICE NG12 lymphoma criterion hinges on lymphadenopathy.
items.fix: Ask directly: "Have you noticed any lumps in your neck, armpits or groin?"

items.fail: Managing entirely by video, with bloods and a review in four weeks.
items.why: You cannot exclude lymphadenopathy or organomegaly remotely, and waiting weeks with B-symptoms is unsafe.
items.fix: Arrange a face-to-face examination within a day or two and put the tests and chest X-ray in place at the same visit.

items.fail: Moving straight on when he admits the lump and his cancer fear.
items.why: "Does not respond to the patient’s cues or emotional content." This disclosure is the emotional centre of the station.
items.fix: Pause: "Thank you for telling me. Carrying that on your own must have been hard." Then explain.

items.fail: Announcing "this could well be lymphoma" with no context, then listing tests.
items.why: Blunt disclosure without hope or structure frightens the patient and is marked as poor explanation.
items.fix: Name the possibility honestly, give the other causes, and say that some lymphomas are very treatable and that quick testing is the next step.

items.fail: Spending eight minutes on a full dermatology and systems review, leaving no time to plan.
items.why: "Poor time management; the plan was insufficiently developed."
items.fix: Focus the history on B-symptoms, lumps, jaundice, drugs and smoking, and be explaining by minute 7.

items.fail: Closing with "come back if it’s no better".
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name the symptoms that need same-day contact, use teach-back, and say you will go through the results yourself.

timeMap.d: He asks for a cream in the first sentence. Acknowledge it, then explain why you need to ask a few questions first.
Night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, itch after a hot bath, jaundice, drugs, smoking. These are the marks, and he will not volunteer them.
Ask directly about lumps. When he discloses the lump and his cancer fear, pause and acknowledge it.
Honest, proportionate explanation. Examination within a day, bloods, chest X-ray, suspected cancer pathway referral if nodes confirmed, symptom relief alongside.
Named symptoms for same-day contact, teach-back, and you will go through results yourself.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a cream or antihistamine on request; never asks about night sweats, weight loss or lumps; no examination arranged; the lump and the cancer fear remain undisclosed; or discloses "it might be cancer" bluntly and leaves him frightened with no plan.
wordPics.pass: Recognises itch without a rash as a systemic flag; elicits the B-symptoms; arranges examination and first-line bloods; mentions urgent referral if nodes are found; gives symptom relief and a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: asks directly about lumps and surfaces the fear with warmth; names lymphoma honestly with realistic hope; links the chest X-ray and referral to NICE NG12 criteria; arranges examination within a day; checks understanding with teach-back and promises personal follow-up.

avoid.instead: "I’ll help with the itch, but itching all over with no rash can come from inside the body, so let me ask a few questions first."
avoid.why: Colluding with the request misses the systemic red flags that define this station.

avoid.dont: "Night sweats, weight loss and a lump: that’s lymphoma until proven otherwise."
avoid.instead: "This pattern is something we take seriously, and one possibility is a problem with the lymph glands. There are other causes too, and checking quickly is how we find out."
avoid.why: Honest but proportionate wording keeps him engaged rather than terrified.

avoid.dont: "Let’s see how the cream goes and review in a month."

I’ll also request a chest X-ray, because you used to smoke and you’ve lost weight. If the lump is what it sounds like, I’ll refer you on the urgent suspected cancer pathway so a specialist sees you quickly. How does that sound?
SCA_MODELS.why: Structured work-up and NICE NG12-based referral plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Quicker than I expected. Better, I suppose.

For the itch meanwhile: a greasy moisturiser used generously, lukewarm rather than hot baths, and I can give you something at night to help you sleep. That makes you comfortable while we find the cause.
SCA_MODELS.why: Symptom relief alongside, not instead of, the work-up

SCA_MODELS.text: If the lump grows quickly, you get fevers, you become breathless, or you feel much more unwell before I see you, ring us the same day, or 111 out of hours. Can you tell me the plan in your own words so I know I’ve explained it clearly?
Come in tomorrow to be examined, bloods and a chest X-ray, possibly an urgent referral, and the cream for the itch. Ring if anything gets worse.
Exactly right. I’ll go through every result with you myself. Would you like someone with you tomorrow?
I’ll think about it. Thanks, doctor. I’m glad I said something.

SCA_STEM.name: Alan Pickering
pmh: No other significant past history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations or blood tests on file. Booked as a video consultation.
SCA_STEM.reason: About 10 weeks of itching all over, worse at night, with no rash. Requesting "a strong cream or antihistamines".

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BAD guidelines for generalised pruritus in adults without an underlying dermatosis (2018) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Generalised itch with no primary rash needs a search for a systemic cause. With night sweats, weight loss and a lump he has noticed, lymphoma must be excluded quickly: examine, test and refer. Symptom relief goes alongside the work-up, never instead of it.

points.t: Scratch marks only, and no primary lesion, point away from a skin disease. Systemic causes include iron deficiency, thyroid disease, chronic kidney disease, cholestatic liver disease, drugs, polycythaemia (itch after a warm bath or shower) and haematological malignancy, particularly Hodgkin lymphoma (BAD 2018).

Drenching night sweats, unintended weight loss, fever and fatigue change the picture. Ask directly, because patients who want a quick cream often leave them out. Also ask whether any lymph node aches after alcohol.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for Hodgkin lymphoma (and non-Hodgkin lymphoma) in adults with unexplained lymphadenopathy, taking into account associated symptoms, particularly fever, night sweats, shortness of breath, pruritus and weight loss (and, for Hodgkin lymphoma, alcohol-induced lymph node pain).
A video consultation cannot rule out lymphadenopathy or an enlarged liver or spleen. Arrange a prompt face-to-face examination of the cervical, axillary and inguinal nodes, abdomen and skin.

BAD 2018: FBC and ferritin in everyone with chronic generalised itch without a rash, with renal, liver and thyroid function. Add a blood film, ESR, LDH, calcium and HbA1c as the picture suggests. NICE NG12: offer an urgent chest X-ray (within 2 weeks) to people aged 40 and over who have ever smoked and have one or more unexplained symptoms such as weight loss or fatigue.

Emollients, cool showers rather than hot baths, and short nails. A sedating antihistamine at night may help sleep in the short term (choice and dose per BNF; caution in older adults). None of this replaces the work-up.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him describe the itch and his request before directing the history.
Impact on sleep and daily life; his reluctance to "make a fuss"; who could come with him.
Picked up the minimising ("just my age"), the pause, and the hot-bath trigger, and followed them.
Idea (dry skin), the hidden concern (a lump and a fear of cancer), and the expectation of a quick cream.
Face-to-face examination of nodes, abdomen and skin; FBC and film, ferritin, renal, liver and thyroid tests, ESR/LDH, calcium; urgent chest X-ray.
Systemic itch: iron deficiency, thyroid, renal, cholestasis, drugs, polycythaemia, lymphoma.
Asked directly for night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, lumps and jaundice; recognised the lymphoma pattern.
Stated a working concern of lymphoma to exclude, with benign causes still possible, in plain language.
Examination within a day, tests, suspected cancer pathway referral if nodes confirmed, symptom relief alongside.
Reviewed medicines and smoking history; gave emollient and sleep advice without delaying the work-up.
Named symptoms that need same-day contact, teach-back, and personal follow-up of results.

social.t: Older men often present a "small" problem and hold back the frightening one. Asking directly and kindly about lumps and weight is what surfaces it.
Offer that someone can come with him to the examination and results appointments; ask about who is at home without assuming.

legal.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely; otherwise arrange a face-to-face assessment. Prescribing on request without assessment is not safe practice.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: share information about possible serious diagnoses honestly and in a way the patient can understand, at a pace he can manage.
Record the suspected diagnosis, the plan and the safety-net. Have a system to track the chest X-ray, bloods and the suspected cancer referral so nothing is lost.

community.t: BAD patient information on pruritus; Lymphoma Action and Macmillan Cancer Support for information and support if lymphoma is confirmed.

redFlags: Drenching night sweats, unintended weight loss, fever, persistent fatigue
A lump in the neck, armpit or groin; node pain after alcohol
Itch after a hot bath (polycythaemia or lymphoma); jaundice, dark urine or pale stools (cholestasis)
psychosocial: Impact on sleep and daily life
Reluctance to "make a fuss"; who is at home to support him
Smoking history and any new medicines or remedies
ice: Idea: "It’s dry skin or my age"
Concern: a lump he has felt, and a fear of cancer he has not voiced
Expectation: a strong cream or antihistamine and to leave

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Generalised itch without a primary rash, with night sweats, weight loss, fatigue and a palpable lump: a systemic cause is likely, and lymphoma must be excluded urgently. Iron deficiency, thyroid, renal and liver disease, polycythaemia and drugs remain in the differential.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: "Itching all over without a rash can be the skin’s way of telling us something is happening inside the body. With the sweats, the weight loss and the lump, I want to check your glands and blood carefully and quickly. It may well be something treatable, but we need to find out."

management.reflectIce: "You came wanting a cream, and you’ve been quietly worried about that lump. I’m glad you told me. Checking it properly is the way to stop you lying awake over it."
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the fear before the plan; offer that someone can come with him; promise to go through results personally.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination within a day: lymph nodes, liver, spleen, skin
FBC and film, ferritin, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, ESR, LDH, calcium, HbA1c; urgent chest X-ray (NICE NG12, ever-smoker aged 40 and over with weight loss or fatigue)
Suspected cancer pathway referral if unexplained lymphadenopathy is confirmed (NICE NG12); emollients and night-time symptom relief meanwhile
safetyNet: Same-day contact for a rapidly growing lump, fever, breathlessness or feeling much more unwell; 111 out of hours
Review of all results with the same GP; track the referral

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by doing what the patient asks. Itch without a rash, B-symptoms and a hidden lump make it a cancer-recognition station dressed as a skin complaint. These are the recurring patterns in SCA feedback.

items.fail: Prescribing an emollient and antihistamine after a two-minute history and closing.
items.why: "Management plan not in line with current UK best practice." Generalised itch without a rash needs a systemic work-up (BAD 2018).
items.fix: Say out loud why you need to ask more: "itching all over with no rash can start inside the body", then screen for B-symptoms.

items.fail: Never asking about lumps, so the node he has felt stays hidden.
items.why: "Did not gather sufficient information to make a safe diagnosis." The NICE NG12 lymphoma criterion hinges on lymphadenopathy.
items.fix: Ask directly: "Have you noticed any lumps in your neck, armpits or groin?"

items.fail: Managing entirely by video, with bloods and a review in four weeks.
items.why: You cannot exclude lymphadenopathy or organomegaly remotely, and waiting weeks with B-symptoms is unsafe.
items.fix: Arrange a face-to-face examination within a day or two and put the tests and chest X-ray in place at the same visit.

items.fail: Moving straight on when he admits the lump and his cancer fear.
items.why: "Does not respond to the patient’s cues or emotional content." This disclosure is the emotional centre of the station.
items.fix: Pause: "Thank you for telling me. Carrying that on your own must have been hard." Then explain.

items.fail: Announcing "this could well be lymphoma" with no context, then listing tests.
items.why: Blunt disclosure without hope or structure frightens the patient and is marked as poor explanation.
items.fix: Name the possibility honestly, give the other causes, and say that some lymphomas are very treatable and that quick testing is the next step.

items.fail: Spending eight minutes on a full dermatology and systems review, leaving no time to plan.
items.why: "Poor time management; the plan was insufficiently developed."
items.fix: Focus the history on B-symptoms, lumps, jaundice, drugs and smoking, and be explaining by minute 7.

items.fail: Closing with "come back if it’s no better".
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name the symptoms that need same-day contact, use teach-back, and say you will go through the results yourself.
